mappings.note: A two-class comparison of solubility in water and in organic solvents. Textbook LO-39: ionic and covalent compounds separated by a property, with nothing formed or computed.

Compare how molecular mass and formula unit mass are computed and which compounds each applies to. LO-39 names exactly that pair; LO-41 would be right only if a number were demanded, as it is in the part-7 item 9f1ff317 that asks for both.
Draw water's shared pairs (LO-40, covalent formation) and justify the subscript in H2O rather than HO (LO-42, formula convention driven by valency). Neither code answers the item alone.
Why ionic solids insulate dry but conduct molten or dissolved. Property-based characterisation, LO-39; the same demand as the short items 53644a5f and 3a60036e, here asked as a single contrast.
Step-by-step valency crossover for calcium chloride. LO-42's method clause applied to a named compound, the same outcome as the aluminium sulfate and aluminium oxide items.

A counterfactual: what would follow if atoms combined in random ratios. Answering it requires explaining what constant proportions buys chemistry, which is LO-40. Not LO-48, which covers stating the concept rather than reasoning from its absence.
Why measured mass appears to fall in an open vessel during a gas-evolving reaction. LO-49's apparent-violation question, stated in general terms rather than through a named reaction.

Both halves are the verification activity: describe the barium chloride/sodium sulfate procedure, then solve the sodium carbonate mass balance. This is LO-39's fused 'plan and demonstrate activities to observe and verify the law of conservation of mass' clause doing all the work; its headline differentiation clause is irrelevant to the item.

Part (a) states the law and names Proust - LO-48 at familiarity level. Parts (b) and (c) illustrate it with water and scale 12 g C : 32 g O down to 6 g of carbon - explanation and application, LO-40. The split within one item is the clearest demonstration of why the two codes are kept apart in this map.
Dalton's postulates behind both laws, plus the indivisibility argument. Entirely inside LO-40, which names Dalton's theory, conservation of mass and constant proportions in a single row.

(a) and (b) are covalent bond definition and the O2 dot diagram - LO-40. (c) asks why covalent compounds melt low, which is the property-based contrast of LO-39. Two genuinely different demands in one five-mark item.
(a) forms the ionic bond in NaCl (LO-40); (b) explains conduction in solution but not solid (LO-39, property). The same two-part shape as 928df894 but on the ionic side.
Criss-cross method described, then applied to aluminium sulfate and calcium carbonate - the second needing the subscripts reduced. All LO-42; the reduction rule has no outcome of its own.

The conductivity rig, copper sulfate against sugar, and the reason for the difference. An ionic-versus-covalent property discrimination, LO-39, with the apparatus serving the comparison rather than verifying a law.

(a) differentiates molecular mass from formula unit mass - LO-39's own pair; (b) then computes one of each - LO-41. This is the model item for how the chapter's mass questions split across the two outcomes, and it needs both.

Predicting the bond from two configurations and explaining the transfer is LO-40; writing the resulting formula is LO-42. Its short-answer counterpart c49adf8b asks for charges instead of mechanism and takes LO-41 plus LO-42.

(a) draws the shell structure from Z=17 - LO-41's 'valency from the atomic number'. (b) contrasts the chloride ion with the neutral atom - LO-39's cation/anion clause. (c) on neon rides on the same configuration argument and adds no third code.

Converts the 3:4 mass ratio in MgS into a 1:1 atom ratio via atomic masses - Dalton's 'relative number of atoms is constant' postulate, which sits in LO-40. Flagged as a weak fit: no outcome in this frame names the mass-ratio-to-atom-ratio conversion, and LO-41's calculation list does not include it.

Mass of one atom scaled by Avogadro's number to an atomic weight, then identified as tungsten. Mapped to LO-41 as the nearest calculation outcome and LO-48 for the particle concept the scaling rests on. POOR FIT: no code in this legal set names the mole, molar mass or Avogadro's number, and LO-41's calculations are enumerated as ion charge, valency and molecular/formula unit mass only.
A limiting-reagent twist on constant proportions: 4 g of X can only take 6 g of Y, so 4 g of Y is left over. LO-40 carries the law; the excess-reagent idea has no outcome anywhere in this curriculum.

(a) and (b) are clean LO-41 and atom-counting from a formula; (c) asks for gram molecules in 18 g of glucose, which is mole arithmetic. LO-48's particle clause is the only thing in the frame that touches counting entities. POOR FIT on part (c) - the mole is absent from every legal code.

Mass of 2.5 moles of CO2 and of 1 mole of water. Purely mole-to-mass conversion. LO-41 is cited because molar mass is numerically the molecular mass it does name, but POOR FIT: the mole itself is unmapped in curriculum 82's frame for this chapter.

Number of water molecules in a 0.05 g drop. The answer is a count of particles, so LO-48's 'matter are made of particles' leads and LO-41 follows for the molar-mass step. POOR FIT: Avogadro's number appears in no legal code.

Mass percentage of Ca, C and O in CaCO3, which runs through the formula unit mass - LO-41's own clause - and then divides. Mild fit issue only: percentage composition is not itself named, but the computation it rests on is.

A closed-vessel precipitation with water carried through, solved for the mass of sodium nitrate. Verification arithmetic on a sealed system - LO-39's fused conservation clause, the same code as the sodium carbonate mass balances.
